The Client and Server lesson introduced several types of servers. Now follow a request to see when each role comes into play. Use the diagram to see when the backend accesses PostgreSQL, Redis, or the file server.

How a web app works

Open a school’s course registration app in your browser. The browser requests the frontend files from the web server and runs them. When you open the course list, the frontend in the browser starts an API request. The browser sends it to the backend over HTTPS and gives the response to the frontend. If you upload a PDF for an enrollment, the backend writes the file to a share on the Samba file server and can record its location with the enrollment in the database.

// Frontend: the browser sends a request to the backend API.
async function loadCourses() {
  const response = await fetch("/api/courses");
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Could not load courses.");
  return response.json();
}
Browser
Downloads and runs the frontend files, then sends API requests initiated by the frontend.
Web Server
Serves the frontend build, including the HTML, JavaScript, and CSS files that the browser needs.
Application Server
Runs the backend API. For a course list request, it returns the course data and can read it from Redis or PostgreSQL.
Cache Server
Redis can temporarily store results such as a course list. The backend can return a cached result when available. On a cache miss, it can query PostgreSQL and cache the new result for a limited time.
Database Server
Runs PostgreSQL, which executes SQL and manages records such as courses and enrollments. PostgreSQL keeps its data files on persistent storage so the records remain after the server process restarts.
File Server
Samba is the file server software in this example. It shares a folder over SMB so the backend can write uploaded PDFs and read them again for downloads.
